channel.title: EEB Daily
channel.description: Nightly one-page evolutionary biology newsletter from the Blackmon lab, Texas A&M.

item.title: No. 11: Fern sugar conduits narrowed through deep time
item.description: Living and fossil fern tissues reveal an evolutionary shift toward narrower sugar-transport cells, with consequences for flow still awaiting direct tests.

item.title: No. 10: Ancient asexuality can scramble a family tree
item.description: A ladder-shaped planarian phylogeny reflects unusual biology.

item.title: No. 9: Mammal genomes break in pairs, and not just anywhere
item.description: Fitting three analytic models of chromosome breakage to synteny blocks from nearly 200 mammal genomes kills the random model outright and leaves two survivors that nobody can yet tell apart.

item.title: No. 8: Catfish that keep rebuilding their sex chromosomes split into species faster
item.description: A genome-wide phylogeny of seventeen Harttia species shows the genus's multiple sex chromosome systems arose at least twice from a simple XY, and the lineages carrying them speciate at a higher rate.

item.title: No. 7: Red opsins keep turning green, and the same four sites do the work
item.description: A third, overlooked LWS paralog in gobies joins the list of lineages that rebuilt green vision from a red-sensitive gene, and the substitutions behind it are the ones primates used.

item.title: No. 6: A foreign block of genome establishes like a single allele
item.description: When an introgressed chunk carries many weakly selected loci, its odds of taking hold ignore recombination entirely; what recombination decides is how much of the block is left standing.

item.title: No. 5: Eighteen origins of gynomonoecy, one crowded receptacle
item.description: In a daisy genus where the textbook explanations do not apply, species that mix female and bisexual flowers in one head pack those flowers twice as densely and make smaller seeds.

item.title: No. 4: When the gene trees disagree, count the fusions
item.description: Nuclear genes and plastomes gave two confident, incompatible answers for a stubborn node in Sapindales; three nested chromosomal fusions give a third, and make it stick.

item.title: No. 3: Antifreeze was the easy part; transposons did the rest
item.description: A phased genome of an Antarctic plunderfish dates the clade's genomic growth, and the growth arrives in lineage-specific bursts rather than with the cold.

item.title: No. 2: Wing shape and venation run on separate clocks
item.description: A self-supervised network reads morphology off raw wing images, and the characters it learns say hymenopteran wings are not tracking the ecology people assumed they track.

item.title: No. 1: Faster-X is not about big mutations
item.description: A new theory said large-effect mutations should drive adaptation on the X. Three genomes say they don't, and the dominance paradox is still standing.
